kernelIdea: Axiom 7: 0 is not the successor of anything, so counting never loops back. Axiom 8: S is injective, so counting never merges. Without them, ℕ = {0} or {0,1} would satisfy everything so far.

kernels.l1: Real counting never comes home, and two numbers never share a next.
kernels.l2: A counting machine that loops back to zero is broken, and so is one where two different numbers have the same next. Two rules forbid exactly those two breakages.
kernels.l3: Two axioms keep counting honest: nothing has 0 as its next, so the count never loops, and no two different numbers share a next, so the count never merges. Without them, a two-element set would pass every earlier axiom.
kernels.l4: Axiom 7 says 0 is not a successor, so counting never returns to the start; Axiom 8 says S is injective, so counting never merges two numbers. Without them ℕ = {0} or ℕ = {0,1} would satisfy every earlier axiom.
kernels.l5: The two axioms rule out looping and merging models; stated in the language of Chapter 3 they say S⁻¹({0}) = ∅ and S is injective.
kernels.l6: Axioms 7 and 8 are exactly the statements that 0 is outside the image of S and that S is injective — a direct reuse of Chapter 3.
kernels.l7: Axiom 7 places 0 outside the image of S and Axiom 8 makes S injective; together they exclude the looping and merging models that satisfy Axioms 1–6, and they yield {0,1,2,…} ⊆ ℕ.
kernels.l8: Axioms 7 and 8 say S is injective with 0 ∉ im(S), i.e. ℕ is a Dedekind-infinite set with a distinguished point; this is Dedekind’s definition of infinity.

kernel: Axiom 7: 0 is not the successor of anything, so counting never returns to the start. Axiom 8: S is injective, so counting never merges two numbers into one.
